issues: The 'NOT SHOWN' label holds: no test here shows a clean excess of dots at DNA ends. What fails is the reason given for it. The ends called 'selection-free' are not free of selection, and two of the quoted below-chance ratios come from the wrong null or a contaminated one. The data neither show nor rule out end attachment; they are not evidence against it.

The rod_no_dot ends are selected AGAINST dots, not free of selection. The W2_2D_rods 2D job used class2D_window_inner_A = 200, a circular window of radius 100 Å around the alignment centre. I placed the aligned box centres from the particle npz (location + shift, using the script's best convention). The L/2+15 Å end points of rod_no_dot rods sit 67 Å from the box centre for the + end (p10-p90 60-74) and 80 Å for the - end (72-86). Both are well inside the window. 'rod_no_dot' is by definition a class with no dot showing, so particles with a visible end dot are pushed into other classes. Below-chance ends are therefore expected even if attachment is real. The dot-class far-end test point sits 95 Å from the box centre (86-110), at the window edge, so it is also partly selected.

The 2D window depletes dots by distance from the box centre, not only by distance from the rod. I took dots 60-90 Å from the rod segment, far from any rod-body effect, in rod_no_dot rods. Their density vs the shift null is 0.59-0.72 at 50-100 Å from the box centre, 0.80-0.95 at 100-140 Å and about 1.0 beyond about 140 Å. For dot classes the same ratio is 0.75-0.86 across 70-150 Å. The shift null re-centres rods in undepleted ice, so its baseline is too high wherever the class window acts. The verdict's 0.71x (rod_no_dot ends) and 0.82x (far ends) are about equal to this local baseline, i.e. about 1.0x locally, not below chance.

Against the null that matches the window baseline, rod_no_dot ends show a small, significant EXCESS, not 'at or below chance'. For rod_no_dot the box centre is only about 6 Å from the rod centre, so the rotation null keeps distance-from-box-centre matched. Against it the ends are: 1.08x at d=35, offset 15 (z=10.5); 1.19x at d=25, offset 15 (z=16.9); 1.27x at d=25, offset 0 (z=22.4); 1.09x with strict dots. Every one has p=0.0099, the minimum possible with 100 replicates. In absolute terms this is only about 1% of rods (0.135 vs 0.125), and part of it may be rod-end false peaks: the along-axis rotation ratio is 1.5-1.8 within ±10 Å of the - end. It is small, but it contradicts the 'at or below chance' wording.

The '0.43x rotation-null' for the far end of dot classes is an artefact. In these classes the pick-centre dot sits about h+17 Å from the rod centre. A rotated virtual end lands within 35 Å of that dot whenever the rotation is within about ±37° of it, which is about 20% of rotations. That inflates the rotation null for both ends equally: minus 0.2275 vs plus 0.2277, against shift-null values of 0.119. This number should not be cited.

A within-rod comparison matched in both distances cannot be built at the attachment distance. I compared end-cap regions (a 45° cone beyond the end) with side regions at the same distance from the rod segment AND the same distance from the box centre. Matched cells exist only for coarse bins, and only from 30 Å from the segment outward. Results: rod_no_dot + end, at 30-40 Å from the rod and 60-80 Å from the box centre, end cap 1.03 vs side 0.86 of the shift null (endcap/side ratio 1.19; 358 end-cap dots, one cell). Dot-class far end, 30-60 Å: ratio 0.99 ± 0.07 (207 end-cap dots). An attached sfGFP centre would sit 10-30 Å beyond the end, and there the side has no counterpart because |t| ≤ 30 Å is excluded. So no fully matched within-rod baseline exists exactly where attachment would show.

The rod set R is not 'independent of whether a dot is present'. R excludes dot_pair_thread (83,949 particles in 5 classes) and dot_pair (37,380). The blind review describes dot_pair_thread as a bright centred dot with a faint second dot or segment 70-100 Å away, sometimes joined by a thread. Those are the shapes a rod with dots at both ends, or a far-end dot, could produce inside a 200 Å window. The far-end and both-ends results are therefore conditioned on these shapes being absent. Both-ends 'no excess' only means that within dot classes P(both) ≈ P(near) × P(far) (0.087 vs 0.082).

Smaller point: only 34 duplicates were removed out of 241,089 rods. Most rods long enough for two picks (min distance 80 Å) are therefore represented by one pick. Which pick survives in R depends on how it classified, and that depends on dots. This is another way union membership depends on dots, and it supports the verdict's point that the union-level enrichment cannot be read as attachment.
skeptics.recommended_wording: An end dot appears in 82% of dot-class rods, but those rods were picked and aligned on the dot, and every other end tested (rod_no_dot ends, dot-class far ends) lies inside the 200 Å 2D-classification window, which selects against visible dots (window depletion 0.6-0.8x of the shift null). Measured against window-matched baselines these ends are about at chance (rod_no_dot ends 1.08-1.27x the rotation null, about 1% of rods; dot-class far ends about the local baseline), so the data neither show nor exclude covalent end attachment. A real test needs a rod set whose class membership cannot see end dots (for example, a body-only mask) or an unreacted-mixture control run through the same pipeline.

issues: Conventions are sound. The pose/shift convention rot(-theta), shift subtracted, particle frame wins clearly: mean r 0.215 against 0.084 for the runner-up and 0.043 with no alignment, and it is the best fit for 78.7% of particles. The micrograph orientation (direct x/y, no flips, r = -0.92, so the stored particle contrast is inverted) is unambiguous. In the QC crops the mapped axes sit on the dark rods. I found no flaw here.

MAIN FINDING: the 'rod_no_dot' classes are not end-dot-free, and their +axis end is misplaced. In 17 of the 21 rod_no_dot class averages, including the biggest ones (57, n=20,917; 58; 1; 170; 74), the along-axis profile peaks 18-37 A INSIDE the +axis half-max end, at 1.5-3.6x the rod level. Class 57 peaks at -18.5 A with 2.55x and class 75 at -31 A with 3.58x. The -axis end of the same classes shows only about 1.1x. That one-ended bright blob is the class-average signature of a dot merged into the rod end. The script puts the rod_no_dot DNA end at the blob's outer half-max edge, not 17 A inside the blob as it does for the dot classes. So that end sits about 35-40 A too far out, and the region where an end-attached sfGFP would actually be (s - L/2 about -20) is classed as 'rod middle'.

The detected dots pile up exactly there. Along the rod_no_dot +axis there are 0.291 dots per rod at s - L/2 in [-35, -5] A (|t| <= 25 A), against 0.048 in the shift null (6.1x; the -20 A bin alone is 13x). The -axis end of the same rods has 0.056 per rod (1.18x), and the inner rod body has 0.026 per rod, below the null's 0.039. The eligibility rule (|s| <= L/2 - 10, |t| <= 30) removes these dots from T and from the nulls. This is why the rod_no_dot ends come out at 1.08x rotation and 0.71x shift, and why the angular end shell (r - L/2 in 10-45 A) shows nothing: both test 30-60 A beyond where the signal is. A misplaced end therefore did wash out an end feature in this stratum.

The verdict reads the on-rod excess as the 'detector firing on rod bodies (0.28/rod, at 35 A spacing = one helical turn)'. The data do not support that. The excess is one-ended and coincides with the class-average maximum, and the rod body and the opposite end are at or below null. The 0.28 per rod is essentially the +end blob (0.29 per rod). A symmetric rod-body or helical artefact would show at both ends. The second peak near -65 A sits at the centre of the longest classes and lines up with a central blob in class 160 (4.9x) and the maxima of classes 58 and 189. It is not a periodic signal.

Because the blob is visible in the rod_no_dot class averages, that end is chosen by class membership, just as in the dot classes. It does not demonstrate attachment, so the NOT SHOWN verdict survives. But the claim that 'rod_no_dot ends' are selection-free is wrong for the +end. Only the rod_no_dot -end and the far end of the dot classes are selection-free.

The rotation null is contaminated by the very dots being tested. Rotating a rod about its centre sweeps its virtual end over the real near-end dot (radius about h + 17 A) and the rod_no_dot blob. For the dot-class far end, the rotation-null histogram peaks at +15 A beyond the end (7,090 against about 1,330 in the shift null). The far-end ratio of 0.43x against the rotation null is therefore deflated and should not be quoted. The shift-null ratio (0.82x) is the fair comparison.

The dot-class far end also has a 2.0x excess just inside the estimated end: 0.113 against 0.055 dots per rod at s - L/2 in [-35, -5], peaking at -30 to -25 A. This zone is excluded from T. It is partly explained by class 78 (n=18,792, the largest dot class), whose average has a bump of 1.99x rod level 24 A inside the far end, which looks like a dumbbell. So 'both ends no excess' holds only outside the excluded zone.

Rod length and 2D mask. W2_2D_rods used class2D_window_inner_A = 200, which soft-masks density beyond 100 A from the alignment centre. In the dot classes that centre sits on the dot, so a flat 170 A duplex would reach about 187 A from it. The dot-class far ends measured 64-99 A from the box centre (several of them 90-99 A), so some far ends may be limited by the mask rather than by the DNA. Even so, the far-end along-axis profile stays at 0.73-0.97x of the shift null all the way out to +120 A, so I see no hidden far-end peak 50-100 A further out. The far-end null result survives the length uncertainty. The rod_no_dot ends (42-79 A from the box centre) are not mask-limited, so their short length (106-146 A) comes from foreshortening or heterogeneity, plus the blob issue above.

Logic limit, briefly: the far-end test only checks whether a SECOND end also carries a dot (a dumbbell or closed loop). A mono-adduct with one sfGFP on one end is fully consistent with the far end being at chance, so a chance-level far end does not argue against single-end attachment.

skeptics.recommended_wording: Selection-free tests give no evidence for covalent end attachment. Dots beyond the far end of dot-at-end rods (0.82x of the shift null, with no excess anywhere out to 120 A) and beyond the -end of rod_no_dot rods are at or below chance, and 2D shows no closed loops. However, most 'rod_no_dot' class averages, like the dot classes, carry a bright blob 20-30 A inside one end, and detected dots pile up there (0.29 per rod, 6x chance, against 1.2x at the other end). So almost every rod class has a one-ended end blob. Because that end is selected by the classification, these data can neither show nor rule out single-end (mono-adduct) attachment; the rod-body false-peak reading and the selection-free status of the rod_no_dot +end should be withdrawn.

issues: The headline still holds: an end-enrichment excess is NOT SHOWN. What fails is the evidence the verdict gives against attachment. The rod_no_dot stratum, used as the 'selection-free' control, is not dot-free. Every large rod_no_dot class average has a bright blob at one end, its +axis end. Its along-axis profile peak is 1.5 to 4.9 times the rod level (class 57: rod level ~60, blob 149; class 75: ~18 vs 62; class 160: 4.86x). The blob sits 18-31 A INSIDE the half-max end. A montage of classes 57, 58, 1, 170, 74, 81, 154, 88, 141, 90, 11, 75, 104, 160 and 46 next to dot classes 4, 31, 35 and 36 shows the same rod-plus-terminal-dot look. The half-max end-finder walks past the blob and puts the DNA end 20-30 A beyond it. For dot classes the opposite rule is used: the end is placed 17 A inside the dot. So the same physical feature counts as 'beyond the end' in one stratum and 'rod body' in the other.

Per particle, 26.7% of the 98,112 rod_no_dot rods have a detected G0 peak in the blob window (10-32 A inside the + end, |t| <= 12 A). The matching window at the - end has 4.3%, and the mid-body has about 1.25e-4 peaks per A^2 against 5.1e-4 per A^2 here. The script's own along-axis histogram shows 13.1x shift-null and 6.3x rotation-null at |s|-L/2 = -18 A on the + side, against 1.2-1.5x on the - side. Every one of these peaks lies in the excluded 'middle region' (|s| <= L/2-10 A). The T window (L/2+15 A, d=35 A) sits 35-45 A beyond them, inside their NMS/LoG shadow: the + side 10-30 A beyond the end holds only 1.1% of rods. So 'rod_no_dot ends 0.135, 1.08x rotation', 'angular end-shell 0.225 vs 0.224' and 'along-axis 10-30 A beyond end 0.65-0.74x' measure the wrong place. They are not evidence of chance-level end occupancy.

The note 'detector fires on rod bodies (0.28/rod, at 35 A spacing = one helical turn)' misreads the profile. The on-rod peaks in rod_no_dot (0.46/rod) are strongly one-sided and concentrated at the + end blob (and at a -62 A bump near the box centre of the long classes). A helical-repeat DNA artefact would be symmetric between the ends of an arbitrarily signed axis. Removing these peaks as rod-body false positives removes exactly the candidate end-attached density.

The far end of the dot classes has the same problem. 8.9% of dot-class rods have a peak 10-32 A inside the measured far end, against 1.4% at 10-30 A beyond it. The along-axis histogram there is 3.05x shift and 2.74x rotation at -22 A. These peaks are also excluded, so the 'far end 0.097, 0.82x shift' and 'both-ends (dumbbell) no excess' results are measured outside where far-end density actually sits. Part of this could be a generic LoG end effect: a uniform ridge gives a response bump about sigma inside its end. But the rod_no_dot + end rate (27%) is 3-6x the other ends' rates (4-9%), so a generic end effect cannot explain most of it.

On selection by 2D on absence: the opposite holds. rod_no_dot classes are not depleted of end dots. They appear to be registered by 2D alignment on a terminal blob, which is the same alignment-on-the-dot selection the verdict rightly blames for the dot-class near-end excess. So rod_no_dot is not an independent, selection-free negative control in either direction.

Detection physics near rods: detected peaks near rods are weaker than isolated ones. Median LoG z is 5.1-5.2 for side windows 25-82 A from the axis, against 6.13 for dots more than 150 A from any rod centre and 6.89 for dot-class end dots. The blob peaks are also weaker (z median 5.46; roundness median 0.56 vs 0.65 background, 10% below 0.35 vs 5%). This fits a partly detection- or region-driven depletion near rods (panel h). It means T near rods is biased low for weak dots. A dot merged with the DNA end in projection is detected (27%) but displaced inward into the excluded zone, so the miss is in the bookkeeping, not the detector itself.

Not a flaw: the detector does find dots sitting just beyond a DNA end. In dot classes, 74% of rods have a peak 10-30 A beyond the + end (z median 6.89). So there is no blanket blindness at ends. The problem is end placement and exclusion, not recall.
skeptics.recommended_wording: The data do not show that sfGFP is attached at DNA ends: the dot-at-end excess in the dot classes comes from picking and 2D alignment on the dot, and there is no selection-free control. The data also do not show the opposite. Most rod_no_dot averages have their own terminal blob, which the end-finder counts as DNA: 27% of rod_no_dot particles have a detected peak 10-32 A inside the measured + end (6x the rotation null), and those peaks are excluded from T as rod body. So the at-chance rod_no_dot, far-end and dumbbell numbers cannot be read as evidence against end attachment.

judge.conclusion: Covalent end attachment is NOT SHOWN, but these data cannot rule it out either. In dot classes, 74% of rods carry a dot beyond one end, but those particles were picked and 2D-aligned on the dot, so the excess comes from selection. The rod_no_dot classes are not a dot-free control. Most of their averages show a bright blob 18-31 Å inside one end, and 27% of their particles have a detected peak there (13x the shift null; 4% at the other end). The end-finder counted the blob as DNA, so those peaks were wrongly excluded as rod-body false peaks. The remaining ends lie inside the 200 Å 2D window and the nulls are biased, so chance-level far-end and both-end counts do not argue against single-end attachment.
followups: Run the free-DNA duplex control (already started through the Fig S6 core) through the same rod picking, 2D (200 Å window) and script-17 steps, then count peaks per rod at each end using one end rule. If DNA-only rods also show the one-ended blob and about 27% one-end peaks, the blob is a DNA or processing artefact. If they do not, the blob goes with sfGFP. An unclicked DNA + sfGFP mixture run the same way would then separate covalent attachment from adsorption or chance proximity. This is the test most likely to change the conclusion.

Place DNA ends the same way in every stratum, without using the blob. For example, fit the rod-body profile away from the ends and use the clean end plus a fixed half-length, rather than half-max points that walk past a terminal blob. Then re-count, per particle, whether 0, 1 or 2 ends have a peak, and compare the + and - ends. Script 17 currently puts the rod_no_dot end beyond the blob but puts the dot-class end 17 Å inside the dot; checked in rod_end_coloc.json along_axis hists: the rod_no_dot + side is 13.1x shift at -17.5 Å, against 1.2-1.5x on the - side.

Replace the nulls with one matched in distance from the box centre and from the rod segment (the local window baseline). Drop the rotation null for dot classes: rotated virtual ends sweep over the real near-end dot, which inflates the null to 0.228 against 0.119 for the shift null and makes the 0.43x far-end ratio an artefact.

Make the end test selection-free. Re-classify rod picks with a body-only mask that excludes about 40 Å at each end, or trace rods on micrographs without classification, so class membership cannot see end dots. Include the dot_pair_thread (83,949) and dot_pair (37,380) classes before testing both-ends (dumbbell) occupancy.
Outside cryo-EM, a denaturing gel or SEC measurement of the DNA-sfGFP conjugate fraction in the crude reaction would set the expected rate of end attachment that these image statistics must match.
